sections.title: The field: EU AI Act, ISO/IEC 42001, UK approach, NIST

facts.text: The EU AI Act is Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, done at Brussels on 13 June 2024. It entered into force on the twentieth day after publication (1 August 2024) and applies generally from 2 August 2026.
facts.quote: It shall apply from 2 August 2026.

facts.text: Original staged dates in Article 113: Chapters I and II (general provisions, AI literacy, prohibited practices) from 2 February 2025; notified bodies, general-purpose AI models, governance and penalties (Chapter III Section 4, Chapters V, VII, XII, Article 78, except Article 101) from 2 August 2025; Article 6(1) from 2 August 2027.

The Commission's AI Act page gives the timeline: entry into force 1 August 2024; prohibitions and AI literacy from 2 February 2025; GPAI and governance rules from 2 August 2025; general application 2 August 2026 with exceptions (page last updated 19 October 2026).

The Commission proposed the AI Omnibus (Digital Omnibus on AI, COM(2025) 836) on 19 November 2025 as part of its digital simplification package; a political agreement was reached on 7 May 2026, and the Omnibus entered into force on 27 July 2026.

The Omnibus was adopted as Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of 8 July 2026, amending Regulations (EU) 2024/1689, 2018/1139 and 2023/1230, and entered into force on the third day after its publication in the Official Journal.
facts.quote: as regards the simplification of the implementation of harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Digital Omnibus on AI)

facts.text: Regulation 2026/1744 amends Article 113: high-risk rules in Chapter III Sections 1 to 3 now apply from 2 December 2027 for Annex III (stand-alone) systems and from 2 August 2028 for Annex I (product-embedded) systems.
facts.quote: 2 December 2027 as regards AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(2) and Annex III

facts.text: Regulation 2026/1744 adds new prohibitions to Article 5 (AI systems generating non-consensual intimate material and child sexual abuse material) applying from 2 December 2026, and gives providers of generative systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 until 2 December 2026 to meet Article 50(2) marking duties.
The original Article 4 required providers and deployers to ensure, to their best extent, a sufficient level of AI literacy of staff, applying from 2 February 2025.
facts.quote: shall take measures to ensure, to their best extent, a sufficient level of AI literacy of their staff

facts.text: Regulation 2026/1744 replaces Article 4: providers and deployers must take measures to support AI literacy, without having to guarantee any specific level; the Commission and Member States must support them, in particular SMEs.
facts.quote: This obligation does not require providers or deployers to guarantee any specific level of AI literacy of any individual.

facts.text: Recital 8 of Regulation 2026/1744 says stringent AI literacy obligations created an additional compliance burden, particularly for smaller enterprises.
Article 11 of the AI Act lets SMEs, including start-ups, provide high-risk technical documentation in a simplified manner using a Commission form.
facts.quote: SMEs, including start-ups, may provide the elements of the technical documentation specified in Annex IV in a simplified manner.

facts.text: The Commission page says the Omnibus extends certain simplified requirements for SMEs, such as simplified technical documentation, to small mid-cap companies, and widens access to regulatory sandboxes, including an EU-level sandbox.
Article 62 requires Member States to give SMEs priority access to AI regulatory sandboxes, run awareness and training tailored to SMEs, and use dedicated communication channels.
Regulation 2026/1744 moves the deadline for each Member State's national AI regulatory sandbox from 2 August 2026 to 2 August 2027.
facts.quote: which shall be operational by 2 August 2027

facts.text: Article 99 sets maximum fines (for prohibited practices up to EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide turnover; for many operator obligations up to EUR 15 million or 3%) and, for SMEs including start-ups, applies whichever amount is lower.
facts.quote: In the case of SMEs, including start-ups, each fine ... shall be up to the percentages or amount ... whichever thereof is lower.

facts.text: Article 26 requires deployers of high-risk AI systems to use them according to instructions and assign human oversight to competent, trained people (these duties follow the high-risk dates in f6).
Article 50 sets transparency duties, for example telling people they are interacting with an AI system unless that is obvious.
The Commission runs an AI Act Service Desk and Single Information Platform with a Compliance Checker (beta) and a question service answered by experts working with the AI Office.

ISO/IEC 42001:2023 (Information technology, Artificial intelligence, Management system), edition 1, published December 2023, sets requirements and guidance for establishing, operating, maintaining and continually improving an AI management system; certification is optional. Read from the iso.org search listing only, as the page itself returned 403.
UK white paper 'A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation' (DSIT and Office for AI, 29 March 2023) sets out a framework for regulating AI.
facts.quote: a proportionate, future-proof and pro-innovation framework for regulating AI

facts.text: The UK government response (6 February 2024, CP 1019) keeps the sector-based approach: existing regulators apply five non-statutory principles (safety, security and robustness; transparency and explainability; fairness; accountability and governance; contestability and redress), with GBP 10 million to build regulator capability, and asked regulators to publish strategic approaches by 30 April 2024.
facts.quote: We will legislate when we are confident that it is the right thing to do.

facts.text: The AI Opportunities Action Plan (DSIT, 13 January 2025, led by Matt Clifford) sets out 50 recommendations to drive AI adoption and growth.
facts.quote: a roadmap for government to capture the opportunities of AI

facts.text: DSIT consulted on the AI Management Essentials (AIME) self-assessment tool from 6 November 2024 to 29 January 2025, inviting in particular start-ups and SMEs.
facts.quote: a self-assessment tool that aims to help organisations assess and implement responsible AI management systems and processes

facts.text: DSIT's government response on AIME (updated 6 February 2026) says it will not publish AIME and will instead develop foundational governance guidance for SMEs deploying AI, and explore templates, online tools and AI Adoption Hubs.
facts.quote: DSIT will not be publishing AIME and therefore will not be making it a requirement of the government procurement process.

facts.text: On 28 January 2026 the DSIT and DBT Secretaries of State wrote to 19 regulators asking each to publish a plan for how they will support safe AI innovation.
facts.quote: publish a plan for how they will support safe AI innovation

facts.text: The Data Protection Act 2018 (Code of Practice on Artificial Intelligence and Automated Decision-Making) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/425) require the ICO to produce a code of practice on personal data in AI and automated decision-making.
The ICO's Guidance on AI and data protection (last updated 15 March 2023) is under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act.
facts.quote: Due to changes made by the Data (Use and Access) Act, this guidance is under review and may be subject to change.

facts.text: The ICO's AI guidance says most uses of AI involve high-risk processing, so a data protection impact assessment (DPIA) will usually be needed; where not, the reasoning should be recorded.
facts.quote: In the vast majority of cases, the use of AI will involve a type of processing likely to result in a high risk

facts.text: The ICO's AI and biometrics strategy, 'Preventing harm, promoting trust', commits to a statutory code of practice on AI and automated decision-making, work on generative AI foundation models, ADM in recruitment and public services, and facial recognition; the page lists a March 2026 update.
facts.quote: Our objective is to empower organisations to use these complex and evolving AI and biometric technologies

facts.text: NIST released the AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0) on 26 January 2023 for voluntary use; its core functions are Govern, Map, Measure and Manage.
facts.quote: intended for voluntary use and to improve the ability to incorporate trustworthiness considerations

facts.text: NIST released the Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1) on 26 July 2024. The NIST page says AI RMF 1.0 is being revised and notes a 7 April 2026 concept note for a critical infrastructure profile.

Synthesis of the sources above (not a single source): what SMEs and their advisers can be asked to show includes a record of AI systems in use and their risk class under the AI Act, AI literacy measures (Article 4), DPIAs where personal data is involved (ICO), transparency notices (Article 50) and, for high-risk uses from December 2027, human oversight and use according to instructions (Article 26). Management-system evidence can be mapped to ISO/IEC 42001 or NIST AI RMF, both voluntary.

sections.title: The market: other readiness tools and services, in their own words

facts.text: UK AI Management Essentials (AIME), DSIT: consulted on as a self-assessment tool for organisations, particularly start-ups and SMEs; DSIT has since said it will not publish AIME and will produce foundational guidance for SMEs instead.
facts.quote: DSIT will not be publishing AIME

facts.text: EU AI Act Compliance Checker, European Commission AI Act Service Desk: free, in beta, describes itself as helping users see which AI Act rules may apply.
facts.quote: helps users understand which AI Act rules may apply to their AI system

facts.text: EU AI Act Compliance Checker and Small Businesses' Guide, Future of Life Institute (not affiliated with the EU): a free checker and an SME guide published 19 February 2025; it advises users to seek professional legal advice.
facts.quote: We have developed this tool voluntarily in order to aid the effective implementation of the AI Act.

facts.text: AIEI (AI Ethics & Integrity International Association) readiness assessments: free, no account, about 15 minutes each, mapped to the EU AI Act, ISO/IEC 42001, ISO/IEC 23894, ISO/IEC 42005, NIST AI RMF and the NIST GenAI Profile; self-assessment only.
facts.quote: Clause-mapped questions against every key framework.

facts.text: BALTUM ISO/IEC 42001 readiness assessment (Estonia): free, 10 to 15 minutes, gives a readiness score, gap analysis, recommendations and a shareable PDF; states it is not a certification body.
facts.quote: The questions are written in plain language, so you do not need a compliance specialist to answer them.

facts.text: SIDD AI Governance Check (Priverion GmbH, Switzerland): a fixed-scope advisory check over 3 to 5 weeks with AI inventory, EU AI Act risk classification, ISO/IEC 42001 gap analysis, roadmap and board summary; published prices from CHF 3'900 (Basic) and CHF 7'500 (Standard, described as for SMEs with genuine AI use).
facts.quote: the standard for SMEs with genuine AI use

facts.text: Neutral contrast (our reading of their own words, not a ranking): the free tools above are self-service and framework-mapped; SIDD is a scoped consultancy engagement; the official checkers focus on whether EU AI Act rules apply. SUSTAIN-NOBILITY presents a short diagnostic plus a review call, a board report, and a licensing tier for advisers serving many SMEs (c4, c8, c9).
